content.title: About
content.content: A fruit smoothie with whole fruit, dairy, and added protein is a nutrient‑dense beverage that blends the natural sweetness of ripe fruit, the creamy texture of milk, and an extra protein boost to support muscle recovery and satiety.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑fruit blends retain fiber, vitamins, and minerals that are lost when using only fruit purées.
Dairy adds calcium and vitamin D, contributing to bone health.
Protein from whey or plant isolates improves the amino‑acid profile of the drink.
Athletes often use fruit smoothies as a quick post‑workout recovery shake.
Varying the fruit mix lets you switch from tropical to berry‑focused flavors.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and antioxidants
items.content: Fruits provide vitamin C, vitamin A, and polyphenols that support immunity and protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: Added protein supplies essential amino acids for muscle repair and growth.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Dairy ingredients help strengthen bones and teeth.

items.title: Fiber for digestion
items.content: Whole fruit retains dietary fiber, promoting healthy gut function.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: The combination of natural fruit sugars and slower‑digesting carbs provides lasting fullness and energy.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: People with these conditions should use plant‑based milk alternatives.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Multiple sweet fruits can raise the drink’s glycemic index; diabetics should monitor portion size.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large amounts of fruit and protein may cause bloating in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Protein and dairy increase calories; consider the portion within your daily energy budget.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Consume the smoothie immediately after blending to preserve vitamin freshness. It works well as a breakfast, post‑workout snack, or light dinner. Add ice for extra refreshment or swap dairy for a plant‑based milk if a lactose‑free option is needed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared smoothie in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. For longer storage, portion and freeze; thaw in the fridge before drinking and give it a quick shake.

content.title: About
content.content: Gin and tonic is a classic cocktail made of gin, tonic water, ice, and often a slice of lime. Gin is a distilled spirit flavored with juniper berries and various botanicals. Tonic water is a carbonated beverage that contains quinine, giving it a distinctive bitter taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recorded combination of gin and tonic dates back to the 19th century, when British officers in India used quinine tonic to prevent malaria.
Traditionally served in a highball glass with plenty of ice and a lime wedge.
There are many gin styles: London dry, botanical-infused (cucumber, rosemary, etc.), and regional varieties, each imparting a unique character.
Tonic can be classic or flavored (berry, citrus, spice) to alter the drink’s profile.
In some countries, a "salted rim" gin‑tonic is popular, where sea salt is sprinkled on the glass edge to enhance flavor.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Quinine in tonic has antioxidant properties, and juniper berries in gin provide flavonoids.

items.title: Moderate consumption may promote relaxation
items.content: Alcohol in moderate amounts can have a calming effect and help reduce stress.

items.title: Vitamin C from lime
items.content: The lime garnish adds vitamin C, supporting the immune system.

items.title: Alcohol
items.content: Excessive alcohol intake can lead to liver issues, dependence, and other health problems.

items.title: Quinine
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to quinine, including rash and headaches.

items.title: Sugar content in tonic
items.content: Many tonic waters contain added sugar, increasing the drink’s calories and affecting blood glucose levels.

content.title: How to Make
content.content: Pour 50 ml of gin into a glass, fill with ice, add 150–200 ml of tonic water, stir gently, and garnish with a lime or lemon wedge. Optional additions include a sprig of rosemary or a few juniper berries.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the gin bottle in a cool, dark place with the cap tightly sealed. Once opened, keep tonic water refrigerated to preserve freshness and flavor.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato hash browns are a ready‑to‑heat product made from grated potatoes, onion and spices, formed into small patties. They are pre‑fried and flash‑frozen, allowing quick preparation in a microwave or oven.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hash browns are a staple in Eastern European cuisine, especially in Poland and Russia.
The frozen product can be stored for up to 12 months when kept properly in a freezer.
For a crispy exterior, bake at 200 °C (390 °F) for 10‑12 minutes.
A small amount of vegetable oil is often added to improve flavor and texture.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes provide starch that offers sustained energy and satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Hash browns contain vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes are a good source of potassium, which supports normal blood pressure.

items.title: Low in fat when prepared without added oil
items.content: If reheated without extra oil, hash browns remain relatively low‑calorie.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to potatoes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some versions contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Heating requirements
items.content: Insufficient heating can leave the interior cold, increasing the risk of food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the hash browns in a microwave (2‑3 minutes) or bake until golden brown. Serve with sour cream, yogurt dip, fresh herbs, or as a side to meat dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen hash browns in an airtight bag at –18 °C (0 °F). Once thawed, cook immediately and do not store at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey fat is the fat from turkey, collected from the skin and body cavity and often rendered into a clear, soft cooking fat. It has a mild poultry flavor and is used for roasting, frying, and flavoring dishes, and for basting poultry. Like other poultry fats, it is softer at room temperature than beef or mutton fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey fat is a by-product of roasting or butchering turkey and can be rendered into a clear fat.
Poultry fats are softer at room temperature than beef or mutton fats because they contain more unsaturated fat.
Turkey fat is often saved from the roasting pan to make gravy or to cook vegetables and potatoes.
It has a moderate smoke point and a mild poultry flavor.
Rendered poultry fats such as schmaltz have been used in Jewish and Eastern European cooking for generations.

items.title: Concentrated energy
items.content: Turkey fat is a calorie-dense source of energy.

items.title: Mostly unsaturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef and mutton fat, turkey fat contains more unsaturated fat.

items.title: Adds flavor
items.content: A small amount adds richness and savory flavor to roasted vegetables, potatoes, and grains.

items.title: Contains fat-soluble vitamins
items.content: Turkey fat contains small amounts of vitamin E and vitamin A.

items.title: Cooking versatility
items.content: It can be used for roasting, sautéing, and basting.

items.title: High in calories and saturated fat
items.content: Turkey fat is calorie-dense and still contains saturated fat, so portions should be small.

items.title: Cholesterol
items.content: Animal fats contain cholesterol, which matters for people with certain health conditions.

items.title: Overheating and reuse
items.content: Heating fat past its smoke point or reusing it many times can produce harmful compounds and bad flavors.

items.title: Spoilage and allergies
items.content: Poultry fat can spoil and turn rancid, and people with poultry allergy should avoid it.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use turkey fat in small amounts to roast potatoes and vegetables, sauté, make gravy, or baste poultry. It can be rendered by slowly melting trimmed fat and straining it. Use it in moderation and avoid heating it until it smokes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store rendered turkey fat in an airtight container in the refrigerator for a few weeks or freeze it for several months. Keep it away from light and heat. Discard fat that smells rancid, sour, or off.
